title: Taking the hukam
hook: the Granth is opened at random and the first hymn on the left page read

segments.voice: Yesterday, what may be sung: in the sangat, Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal, and nothing else. Your line was only the word. Which line did you keep humming? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

Nobody picks the page. That's the first thing to know. The Granth has been opened at dawn, as we saw two days ago, and now the reader sits behind it, hands resting on the cloth. The sangat waits. The reader doesn't flip to a favorite hymn or a passage that suits the news. The Granth is opened where it opens. Then the reader's eyes go to one particular place on the page, and whatever is written there is read aloud to everyone in the hall. It has a name, and some gurdwaras write it on a board by the door for anyone who missed it.
screen: `NOBODY PICKS THE PAGE.` → `OPENED WHERE IT OPENS.` → `READ ALOUD TO THE HALL.`

segments.voice: We've brushed past this twice already, with the Tenth Guru's letters and with the sticky note on the mirror. Today, the method. The word is hukam: order, command. What's read is called the hukam, or the hukamnama, the written order. In paraphrase, the code gives the method. Open the Granth at random. Read the hymn at the top of the left-hand page. If that hymn began on the page before, turn back and read it from its beginning. The hymn is read whole, not cut off where the page happens to start. Now, why call it an order? Because the word hukam goes back to the very first page of the Granth. Japji Sahib asks how a person can become truthful, how the wall of falsehood can be broken. And it answers, in paraphrase: by walking in the hukam, the Will, which is written along with us. So for Sikhs, hukam isn't a boss's memo. It's the Will that orders everything, the way the tide is ordered and the seasons are. The daily hukam is a small, concrete window onto that. One hymn, received rather than chosen, heard as the Guru's word for this day. It's easy to mistake this for fortune-telling, and that's not how it's understood. The hukam doesn't predict anything. For Sikhs, every page of the Granth is the Guru's word, so wherever it opens, the Guru speaks. What changes is the listening. A Sikh who takes the hukam in the morning carries one hymn into the day and lets the day be read in its light. Some Sikhs read the day's hukam from a gurdwara on their phone before work. It's the same idea: not a forecast. The order of the day.
screen: `HUKAM: ORDER, COMMAND.` · `THE LEFT PAGE, FROM THE HYMN'S START.` · `JAPJI: WALK IN THE HUKAM.` · `NOT A FORECAST: THE GURU SPEAKS.` · then, large: `THE ORDER OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read today's hukam. Settle, and breathe. If you can, find today's hukam from a gurdwara and read it slowly, once. If you can't, take any line of scripture or wisdom you didn't choose for yourself, from a book opened where it falls. Don't analyze it yet. Read it, then close your eyes and let one phrase stay. Hold that phrase as if it were addressed to today, and only today. Rest with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Taking the hukam. Opening the Granth at random and reading the first hymn on the left-hand page, from its beginning: the Guru's order for the day. Today's word.
Your line: the order of the day. Today, carry one received line with you, and at noon and at night, ask what it said about the hours in between. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: After the Granth is opened in the morning, the granthi opens it at random and reads the hymn at the top of the left-hand page as the hukam; some gurdwaras display it by the door or share it online.

notes: The code's method is paraphrased: open at random, read the hymn at the top of the left-hand page, turning back to its start if it began on the previous page. The code also gives guidance for vars (reading a pauri with its sloks), left out here for simplicity. Please confirm.
Japji pauri 1 (Ang 1) paraphrased: how to become truthful and break the wall of falsehood? by walking in the hukam, the Will, written along with us. Please confirm.
The 'not fortune-telling' framing is offered as how Sikhs understand the hukam; please confirm it is fair.
'Some Sikhs read the day's hukam from a gurdwara on their phone' and 'some gurdwaras write it on a board by the door': general descriptions; please confirm.
